name: Mauryan Empire
summary: An early subcontinental empire founded in Magadha and expanded through conquest and diplomacy under Chandragupta, Bindusara, and Ashoka.
capital: Pataliputra
military: Conquest extended authority from the Ganges basin into northwestern and central South Asia.
contributions: Ashoka’s inscriptions preserve early evidence of imperial administration and ethical policy; his patronage helped spread Buddhism.
origin: Chandragupta displaced the Nanda dynasty in Magadha.
decline: The empire fragmented within roughly fifty years of Ashoka’s death.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art — Mauryan Empire
University of Washington — The Mauryan Empire

periodNote: Foundation is approximate: sources use c. 323 or c. 321 BCE. Ashoka’s accession dates also vary.

name: Gupta Empire
summary: A northern Indian dynasty whose imperial expansion supported influential developments in Sanskrit literature, visual art, mathematics, and astronomy.
capital: Pataliputra; Ujjain was also an important royal and commercial centre.
rulers: Selected: Chandragupta II, c. 375–415; Kumaragupta I, 415–454; Skandagupta, 455–467.
economy: Agriculture, trade, and port connections supported imperial revenue; military pressures and land assignments strained later finances.
military: Campaigns expanded Gupta power across northern India; conflicts with Huna forces weakened later rulers.
contributions: Patronage of Sanskrit literature and sculpture; the period saw major advances in astronomy and mathematics.
origin: The dynasty developed into an imperial power in northern India during the early fourth century.
decline: Huna incursions, dynastic conflict, and the independence of subordinate rulers undermined central authority.

sources.title: INFLIBNET — The Gupta empire
Smarthistory — The Gupta Period
IGNCA — The Gupta and Post-Gupta periods

periodNote: c. 320–550 refers to imperial Gupta power, not the longer Gupta cultural period.

name: Chola Empire
summary: A Tamil dynasty centred on the Kaveri delta, with extensive South Indian power, overseas campaigns, and lasting temple and bronze traditions.
capital: Thanjavur; Gangaikondacholapuram from the reign of Rajendra I (district history dates its capital role to 1027).
economy: The Kaveri delta and merchant towns supported agriculture and trade; merchant guilds linked regional and overseas markets.
military: Armies expanded across southern India and Sri Lanka; diplomacy and alliances complemented conquest.
contributions: Monumental temples, bronze casting, and distinctive Tamil court and religious art.
origin: The Chola ruling family re-established regional dominance in the mid-ninth century.

sources.title: Smithsonian — Chola Dynasty
Ariyalur District — History
UNESCO — Great Living Chola Temples

periodNote: c. 850 marks the medieval imperial revival, not the earlier Chola lineages. 1279 is the conventional end of the last imperial Chola reign.

name: Delhi Sultanate
summary: Successive sultanates based at Delhi that extended political authority across much of northern India and, intermittently, into the Deccan.
capital: Delhi, across successive royal cities.
economy: Regional markets and monetization supported the sultanates; land revenue sustained administrative and military service.
military: Military households and commanders governed assigned territories; expansion included campaigns toward the Deccan.
contributions: Persianate court culture, urban construction, manuscript patronage, and expanded commercial networks.
origin: Turkish military rulers established independent authority in northern India in the early thirteenth century.
decline: Regional fragmentation weakened Delhi; Babur defeated the Lodi sultan in 1526.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica — Delhi Sultanate
NCERT via IIT Kanpur — Delhi: 12th to 15th Century
The Met — Wonder of the Age

periodNote: An umbrella for five ruling dynasties, not an uninterrupted uniform territorial state. Iltutmish’s accession is also dated 1211.

name: Mughal Empire
summary: A dynasty founded by Babur and consolidated by Akbar, whose power eventually encompassed much of the Indian subcontinent.
capital: Major imperial seats included Agra, Delhi, and Lahore; the court also moved between residences.
currency: Silver rupee, gold mohur, and copper dam; the system developed from Sher Shah’s monetary reforms.
economy: Commercial centres, especially Gujarat, connected the empire to Arabian Sea trade and supplied substantial wealth.
military: Military conquest established the dynasty; territorial consolidation under Akbar combined campaigning with administrative integration.
contributions: Imperial painting, architecture, and manuscript production; consolidation of widely used coinage.
origin: Babur defeated the Delhi sultan’s forces in 1526; Akbar subsequently consolidated imperial institutions.
decline: Later emperors became largely nominal rulers; British authorities deposed Bahadur Shah Zafar after the 1857 uprising.

sources.title: The Met — The Art of the Mughals before 1600
Reserve Bank of India — Mughal Coinage
The Met — Islamic Art Teaching Resource, Unit 5

periodNote: Rule was interrupted by the Sur dynasty, 1540–1555. 1857 marks the last emperor’s deposition; some timelines use 1858.

name: Maratha Empire
summary: A polity built under Shivaji that expanded under the Peshwas and increasingly operated through powerful regional houses.
capital: Raigad under Shivaji; Pune became the Peshwas’ political centre.
currency: Multiple rupee standards, including Hali Sicca, Ankushi, and Chandori issues.
economy: Land-revenue claims, including chauth and sardeshmukhi, helped finance expansion; regional towns and trade developed under Maratha rule.
military: Mobile forces drew heavily on peasant-pastoral communities; regional chiefs became increasingly powerful.
contributions: New regional political institutions, revenue networks, and urban centres across western and central India.
origin: Shivaji established a Deccan kingdom through warfare and alliances; his coronation in 1674 formalized kingship.
decline: Regional competition and wars with the East India Company culminated in the Peshwa’s defeat in 1818.

sources.title: NCERT via IIT Kanpur — Eighteenth-Century Political Formations
Reserve Bank of India — Coins of the Indian Princely States
Maharashtra Gazetteers — The Maratha Period
Cambridge — Pacification and Patronage in the Maratha Deccan, 1803–1818

periodNote: 1674 marks Shivaji’s coronation, not the start of his conquests. Maratha-ruled princely states survived the confederacy’s defeat in 1818.

name: Sikh Empire
summary: Ranjit Singh consolidated competing Sikh confederacies into a kingdom centred on Lahore and expanded across Punjab and neighbouring regions.
capital: Lahore
currency: Silver rupees, including Nanakshahi issues; copper coins also circulated.
rulers: Selected: Ranjit Singh, 1799–1839; assumed the title Maharaja in 1801.
economy: Ranjit Singh’s court supported trade, luxury crafts, and artistic patronage.
military: A substantial army supported territorial expansion and diplomacy with British and Afghan neighbours.
contributions: Patronage of Punjabi court arts, architecture, and crafts within a religiously diverse kingdom.
origin: Ranjit Singh captured Lahore in 1799 and consolidated power among Sikh misls.
decline: The kingdom collapsed within a decade of Ranjit Singh’s death; British conquest ended sovereignty in 1849.

sources.title: Royal Welsh Museum — The Sikh Empire
Wallace Collection — Maharaja Ranjit Singh
State Bank of Pakistan — Sikh Rulers
National Army Museum — Maharaja Ranjit Singh

periodNote: 1799 marks the capture of Lahore; 1801 marks Ranjit Singh’s proclamation as Maharaja.

name: Qin Empire
summary: The first imperial unification of China, built by a formerly regional Qin state through conquest and administrative centralization.
capital: Xianyang.
rulers: Selected: Qin Shi Huang, 221–210 BCE as emperor.
economy: Land reform, resettlement, standardized measures, and road-building supported centralized administration.
military: Broad male military service and sustained conquest made Qin the leading power among competing states.
contributions: Standardized writing, weights, measures, and currency; enduring models for imperial administration.
origin: The Qin state conquered rival kingdoms and proclaimed an emperor in 221 BCE.
decline: Rebellion after the first emperor’s death brought down the dynasty and opened the struggle from which Han rule emerged.

sources.title: The Met — Age of Empires exhibition galleries
Smithsonian — Timeline of Chinese History, Art, and Culture
UNESCO — Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

periodNote: Dates describe the imperial Qin dynasty, not the much older Qin regional state; some chronologies end it in 207 BCE.

name: Han Empire
summary: A long-lived imperial dynasty that developed the Qin administrative inheritance and connected China to wider Eurasian exchange.
capital: Chang’an during Western Han; Luoyang during Eastern Han (25–220).
rulers: Selected: Gaozu (Liu Bang), 202–195 BCE as emperor.
economy: Road networks, a centralized administration, and long-distance exchange supported imperial integration.
contributions: Imperial institutions, historical writing, and developments in paper-making and long-distance exchange.
origin: Liu Bang emerged from rebellion against Qin and became emperor after the ensuing civil struggle.
decline: Central authority collapsed and the empire divided into competing kingdoms.

sources.title: The Met — Age of Empires
Smithsonian — Timeline of Chinese History, Art, and Culture
Princeton University Art Museum — China Timeline
The Met — Han Dynasty

periodNote: 206 BCE marks Liu Bang’s kingship; imperial rule began in 202 BCE. Han rule was interrupted by Wang Mang’s Xin dynasty (9–23 CE).

name: Tang Empire
summary: A cosmopolitan Chinese empire whose expanding administration, trade networks, and court culture influenced much of East Asia.
capital: Chang’an was the principal early imperial capital.
economy: Overland trade and urban exchange brought merchants and products from across Eurasia to the capital.
military: Early rulers campaigned against northern and northwestern neighbours; military rebellion later weakened central power.
contributions: Poetry, painting, ceramics, and civil-service examinations developed enduring influence.
origin: Li Yuan founded the dynasty after the collapse of Sui authority.
decline: The An Lushan rebellion weakened the court; subsequent fragmentation culminated in the dynasty’s collapse.

sources.title: The Met — Tang Dynasty
Smithsonian — Timeline of Chinese History, Art, and Culture
University of Washington — Tang dynasty

periodNote: The usual 618–907 span includes the interruption of Tang dynastic rule by Wu Zetian’s Zhou dynasty (690–705).

name: Song Empire
summary: A Chinese imperial state known for commercial and urban growth, scholarly government, technological change, and influential painting and ceramics.
capital: Bianliang (Kaifeng) in the Northern Song; Lin’an (Hangzhou) in the Southern Song.
currency: Metal coins and paper currency, including jiaozi and later huizi.
economy: Expanding commerce encouraged monetary innovation and the circulation of paper money.
military: Jurchen conquest forced the court south in 1127; Mongol conquest ended Southern Song rule in 1279.
contributions: Paper currency, scholar-official culture, landscape painting, and advances in ceramics.
origin: The dynasty restored political unity after the Five Dynasties period, while neighbouring states retained substantial territories.
decline: Jurchen expansion removed the northern heartland; the Mongols subsequently conquered the remaining southern state.

sources.title: The Met — Northern Song Dynasty
The Met — Southern Song Dynasty
Columbia University — Song economic revolution: money
Smithsonian — Timeline of Chinese History, Art, and Culture
American Numismatic Association — An Experiment in Paper

periodNote: Northern Song: 960–1127; Southern Song: 1127–1279. These are phases of one dynasty with substantially different territories.

name: Yuan Empire
summary: The Mongol-ruled dynasty in China, centred on Dadu and embedded in wider Eurasian networks of trade and political exchange.
capital: Dadu (Khanbaliq; present-day Beijing).
currency: Paper money, initially supported by a silver standard; monetary policy changed over time.
rulers: Selected: Kublai Khan, 1271–1294 as Yuan emperor (Great Khan from 1260).
economy: A unified monetary regime supported exchange; imperial finances and paper-money stability deteriorated later.
military: Mongol conquest absorbed the Southern Song in 1279.
contributions: Eurasian cultural exchange, new developments in ceramics, and influential literati painting.
origin: Kublai’s Mongol regime adopted the Yuan dynastic name before completing the conquest of Southern Song.
decline: Factional conflict, fiscal disorder, disasters, and rebellion undermined the court; Ming forces took the capital in 1368.

sources.title: The Met — Yuan Dynasty
University of Manchester — The rise and fall of paper money in Yuan China
Smithsonian — Timeline of Chinese History, Art, and Culture

periodNote: 1271 marks the dynastic proclamation; some histories use 1279, when Song conquest ended. The Northern Yuan continued after the loss of China in 1368.

name: Ming Empire
summary: A Chinese dynasty established after the overthrow of Yuan rule, associated with major imperial building, overseas expeditions, and artistic production.
capital: Nanjing initially; Beijing from 1421.
currency: Paper notes, with increasing reliance on silver and copper coinage.
economy: Artisanal production and overseas trade connected Chinese manufactures to wider markets; silver became important in taxation.
military: Naval expeditions under Zheng He reached the Indian Ocean and East African coast.
contributions: The Forbidden City, influential porcelain production, painting, lacquerwork, and maritime expeditions.
origin: Zhu Yuanzhang led a successful rebellion against the Yuan and proclaimed the Ming in 1368.

sources.title: The Met — Ming Dynasty
Smithsonian — Timeline of Chinese History, Art, and Culture
British Museum via Smarthistory — Ming banknote
Columbia University — China, 1450–1750
Ghent University — The Shandong Peninsula in East Asian Maritime History
Palace Museum — Hongwu Emperor

periodNote: 1644 marks the fall of Beijing and the main Ming court; Southern Ming regimes continued after this date.

name: Qing Empire
summary: A Manchu-led empire governing China and extensive Inner Asian territories, and the final dynasty of imperial China.
capital: Beijing.
currency: Copper coins and silver, with changing late-imperial monetary arrangements.
economy: A largely agricultural economy with extensive markets, merchant networks, and growing links to global silver trade.
military: Manchu military institutions remained central to the dynasty; military service had a hereditary component.
contributions: Court patronage, encyclopedic and artistic projects, and extensive commercial and cultural exchange.
origin: Manchu rulers conquered Beijing in 1644 and extended power over the former Ming realm.
decline: The 1911 revolution ended imperial rule; the last emperor abdicated in 1912.

sources.title: National Library of Australia — Emperors
Columbia University — Qing economy
Princeton University Art Museum — China Timeline
Smithsonian — Timeline of Chinese History, Art, and Culture

periodNote: The Qing name was adopted in 1636; 1644 marks entry into Beijing. Museum chronologies sometimes end in 1911, the revolution year, rather than the 1912 abdication.

name: Mongol Empire
summary: A rapidly expanding empire created by Chinggis Khan’s unification of steppe peoples, connecting large parts of Eurasia through conquest and exchange.
capital: A mobile royal court initially; Karakorum developed as an imperial capital under Ögödei in the 1230s.
economy: Pastoral resources, taxation, tribute, and long-distance trade supported imperial expansion and consumption.
military: Highly mobile mounted forces conducted successive campaigns across Eurasia; conquered populations also supplied personnel and expertise.
contributions: Expanded Eurasian travel, commerce, and exchanges of skills and knowledge, alongside extensive destruction and forced displacement.
origin: Temüjin united rival steppe groups and was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206.
decline: Succession conflicts and competing dynastic interests produced civil war and the division of authority among successor khanates.

sources.title: Cambridge — The Rise of Chinggis Khan and the United Empire, 1206–1260
University of Washington — Mongol chronology
Royal Armouries — Rise of the Mongols
Columbia University — Collapse of the Empire

periodNote: This record uses the united empire, 1206–1260. Successor khanates and nominal claims to unity continued; 1260 is not the end of all Mongol rule.

name: Khmer Empire
summary: An Angkor-centred mainland Southeast Asian state supported by agricultural production, water infrastructure, and powerful royal and temple institutions.
capital: Angkor for most of the period; Koh Ker was a rival capital from 921 and the sole capital during 928–944.
currency: Exchange was not primarily coin-based; imported Chinese coins had varied uses.
economy: Agricultural production, labour obligations, and extensive water management supported royal and temple establishments.
contributions: Monumental temple architecture, urban water infrastructure, sculpture, and connected regional artistic traditions.
origin: Later inscriptions associate 802 with Jayavarman II’s assertion of kingship and consolidation of regional power.
decline: Political and economic reorientation occurred gradually, with environmental pressures and changing regional power relationships; a single catastrophic collapse is misleading.

sources.title: National Library of Australia — Rise of Angkor
National Library of Australia — Decline of the Khmer Empire
PNAS — Geoarchaeological evidence from Angkor
Asian Archaeology — Chinese coins in Angkor
UNESCO — Koh Ker

periodNote: 802 and 1431 are conventional period markers. Archaeology indicates gradual transformation, not a precise empire-wide disappearance in 1431.

name: Srivijaya
summary: A maritime polity centred in southern Sumatra, exercising influence through port networks and trade routes linking the Indian Ocean and China.
capital: Palembang and later Jambi are associated with its political centres; the chronology remains debated.
economy: Port commerce and control of maritime connections supported its power.
contributions: Facilitated maritime exchange and Buddhist travel and scholarship across Asian networks.
origin: A powerful port-centred polity emerged in southern Sumatra during the later seventh century.
decline: Chola attacks and the growing autonomy of competing ports reduced its influence; its final disappearance cannot be assigned confidently to one event.

sources.title: Oxford World History of Empire — Śrīvijaya
Singapore National Library Board — Sang Nila Utama
Getty Research — Srivijaya

periodNote: c. 670–1300 is an approximate display span, not established foundation and dissolution years. Sources define Srivijaya’s later continuity differently.

name: Majapahit Empire
summary: An East Javanese kingdom with a sophisticated court and extensive regional connections, centred for much of its history on Trowulan.
capital: Trowulan; a later court at Daha is recorded after 1478.
currency: Local and imported coins are attested archaeologically at Trowulan.
economy: Irrigated agriculture, markets, craft production, and regional exchange supported the capital and surrounding settlements.
contributions: Urban water engineering, sculpture, terracotta production, and distinctive architecture.
origin: The kingdom was established in eastern Java in 1293.
decline: Dynastic conflict and shifting regional power eroded its position; successor Islamic polities became increasingly influential.

sources.title: UNESCO tentative list — Trowulan
Direktori Majapahit — Sejarah Kerajaan Majapahit
Universitas Indonesia — Cultural resource management at Trowulan
Direktori Majapahit — Inspiration for the World

periodNote: The end date is disputed: 1478, c. 1500, c. 1520, and 1527 appear in institutional chronologies. 1527 follows Direktori Majapahit; territorial authority contracted earlier.

name: Mali Empire
summary: A West African empire that linked the upper Niger region to trans-Saharan trade and supported influential centres of scholarship and material culture.
economy: Gold, salt, and trans-Saharan commerce supported imperial prosperity; river routes connected regional exchange.
contributions: Patronage of scholarship and architecture; integration of diverse communities into extensive commercial and cultural networks.
origin: Expansion under Soundiata Keita transformed an upper Niger kingdom into a major imperial power.
decline: Succession disputes and secession weakened the empire, while Songhai absorbed important northern trade centres.

sources.title: The Met — Sahel exhibition
Smithsonian — From Golden Age Empires to Independence
Embassy of Mali in Japan — History
The Met — Western and Central Sudan, 1400–1600

periodNote: c. 1230–1600 follows the Met’s broad imperial period. The location and continuity of the imperial capital remain debated; decline was gradual.

name: Songhai Empire
summary: A Niger River empire centred on Gao that expanded over major Sahelian commercial and scholarly cities during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
capital: Gao
economy: Trans-Saharan trade and control of gold, salt, and copper routes supported imperial power.
military: Cavalry and river fleets enabled expansion; Moroccan forces armed with firearms defeated the imperial army in 1591.
contributions: Patronage made Timbuktu a major centre of scholarship and manuscript production.
origin: Songhai expanded as Mali’s authority weakened, under military leaders including Sonni Ali.
decline: Internal divisions weakened the empire; the Moroccan invasion and defeat at Tondibi in 1591 ended its regional supremacy.

sources.title: The Met — Sahel exhibition
The Met — Western and Central Sudan, 1400–1600
Library of Congress — Timbuktu: An Islamic Cultural Center

periodNote: 1464 marks the major imperial expansion, not the older Songhai state. Resistance and successor authorities survived 1591.

name: Kingdom of Aksum
summary: A northeastern African state linking the Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands with Red Sea commerce and, at times, southern Arabia.
capital: Aksum
currency: Gold, silver, and copper coinage; minting began in the late third century.
economy: Agriculture and commerce through Red Sea connections supported the kingdom.
military: Royal campaigns extended power beyond the highlands, including into southern Arabia at its height.
contributions: Monumental stelae, distinctive architecture and coinage, and an enduring written and Christian cultural legacy.
origin: An urban trading and political centre developed in the northern Ethiopian highlands during the early first millennium.
decline: Changing Red Sea trade and environmental pressures contributed to political and economic reorganization; the process was gradual and remains debated.

sources.title: UNESCO — Aksum
The Met — Foundations of Aksumite Civilization
The Met — Monumental Architecture of the Aksumite Empire
French Ministry of Culture — La fin du royaume
British Museum via Smarthistory — Aksumite coins

periodNote: 1–800 is a century-level display range for the first through eighth centuries, not precise foundation and dissolution years. Aksum’s political transformation has no universally agreed endpoint.

name: Ethiopian Empire
summary: A highland monarchy whose changing institutions and territories linked medieval Christian kingship to the Ethiopian imperial state of the twentieth century.
capital: Mobile royal camps initially; Gondar from 1636; Addis Ababa under Menelik II and later emperors.
currency: Multiple historical media; birr-denominated issues are documented under Haile Selassie.
rulers: Selected: Amda Seyon I, 1314–1344; Haile Selassie I, 1930–1974.
economy: Landholding, agricultural taxation, and commerce sustained the monarchy; twentieth-century centralization depended on expanding tax revenue.
contributions: Distinctive architecture, manuscript and artistic traditions, and enduring institutions of Ethiopian statehood.
origin: Yekuno Amlak established the Solomonic ruling line in 1270, drawing on earlier highland kingdoms.
decline: Military officers deposed Haile Selassie in 1974 and replaced imperial government.

sources.title: Wachemo University — History of Ethiopia and the Horn
UNESCO — Gondar palaces and castles
Library of Congress — Ethiopia: A Country Study
National Bank of Ethiopia — Banknotes
Addis Ababa Mayor’s Office — City history

periodNote: 1270 identifies the Solomonic dynasty, not the beginning of Ethiopian statehood. Italian occupation interrupted imperial administration in 1936–1941; 1974 marks the emperor’s deposition.

name: Zulu Kingdom
summary: A southern African kingdom consolidated under Shaka, whose regional power endured until British invasion dismantled its sovereignty.
economy: Cattle were central to wealth, status, food supply, marriage exchanges, and political relationships.
military: A powerful army resisted the British invasion of 1879, defeating a British force at Isandlwana before later defeats.
origin: Shaka consolidated and expanded the Zulu kingdom from 1816.
decline: British victory in 1879 led to Cetshwayo’s removal and territorial partition; restricted restoration was followed by British annexation in 1887.

sources.title: South African History Online — Zulu Family History
National Army Museum — Zulu War
University of Cape Town archive — uMgungundlovu archaeology
University of Zululand — Research on Shaka’s state

periodNote: 1816–1879 describes the consolidated independent kingdom. Cetshwayo returned with reduced powers in 1883; British annexation followed in 1887. The monarchy continues as a traditional institution.
